evals.prompt: Our public REST API (a SaaS for managing event venues) has no rate limiting. Big customers hammer /v1/bookings with polling scripts and last month a runaway integration took down the API for everyone. Write a design document for adding rate limiting to the public API. Context you can assume: Python/FastAPI behind an AWS ALB, Redis is available, API-key auth per tenant, team of 4 engineers will review and implement this. Save the document as rate-limiting-design.md in the current directory.
evals.expected_output: An API-flavored design doc: objective, evidence-based background, goals/non-goals, limit model and enforcement point, exact 429 contract with headers and typed error shape, client retry guidance, rollout plan, open issues, brief alternatives. No invented traffic numbers.
assertions: Document opens with metadata (status/author/date) and a one-sentence objective
Has an explicit non-goals section
Specifies the exact 429 response contract: a typed/branchable error body shape plus rate-limit headers (e.g. Retry-After or X-RateLimit-*)
Gives client retry guidance (backoff behavior or Retry-After semantics)
Contains an open issues / open questions section with proposed resolutions instead of silently inventing unknown traffic numbers
Contains an alternatives-considered section with at least two rejected options and a stated reason each
Includes at least one editable text-based diagram (e.g. Mermaid) with source inline
Includes a rollout/phasing plan where each phase has a verification gate
Does not fabricate specific current traffic metrics not given in the prompt (any numbers are labeled as assumptions/placeholders or derived from the prompt)

evals.prompt: I'm building a desktop kanban app (Tauri + React). Right now the whole board state lives in a single Redux store and everything is lost if the app crashes; also dragging cards while offline silently drops changes when we reconnect because the server rejects stale writes. I need a design doc for how board state should be owned, persisted, and synced - covering offline edits, conflict handling, crash recovery, and what the UI shows in each of these states. Save it as board-state-design.md in the current directory.
evals.expected_output: A UI/UX state design doc: state ownership table (server truth vs synced cache vs local persisted vs transient), full per-surface state matrix (loading/ready/empty/offline/conflict/error), offline behavior per action, crash recovery, persistence format and migration, honest copy rules, diagrams.
assertions: Document opens with metadata and a one-sentence objective
Contains a state-ownership model (table or equivalent) assigning each state fact exactly one owner and a durability class (server truth / synced cache / persisted local / transient view state)
Defines a per-surface state matrix in which loading, ready/empty, offline, conflict, and error states are all distinct
Specifies offline behavior per user action: what works locally and what disables with a visible reason
Defines conflict handling concretely (not TBD): detection, resolution rule, and what the user sees
Defines crash recovery: what is persisted, where (file/store named), and what the user sees on relaunch
Includes a persistence format and a migration/first-run story
Has explicit non-goals
Includes at least one Mermaid or other text-based diagram (state or data flow)

evals.prompt: My team at an insurance company keeps debating whether we should build an internal 'claims copilot' that drafts claim responses for adjusters using an LLM. Before anyone writes code I want a concept/design doc that frames the problem, what we know and don't know, and how we'd decide whether to build it at all. Context: 120 adjusters, average 25 claims/day each, we have a claims DB, and there is a lot of skepticism from compliance. Save it as claims-copilot-concept.md in the current directory.
evals.expected_output: A conceptual design doc: evidence-vs-interpretation problem framing, core insight, scenarios, principles, risky assumptions each with a cheapest falsification experiment, do-nothing alternative costed, compliance addressed, a path-to-conviction experiment sequence instead of a build plan, no fabricated metrics.
assertions: Document opens with metadata and a one-sentence objective
Problem statement separates observed evidence from interpretation, or explicitly labels unverified claims as assumptions
States a quotable core insight or concept statement (what makes this worth building), not just a feature list
Lists risky assumptions and attaches a concrete cheapest falsification experiment to each
Addresses the do-nothing alternative with an honest cost assessment
Directly addresses compliance concerns (given in the prompt) rather than ignoring them
Ends in a path-to-conviction / experiment sequence with decision points, not an implementation build plan
Has explicit non-goals
Does not fabricate metrics beyond those in the prompt (any derived numbers trace to the prompt's 120 adjusters / 25 claims figures or are labeled assumptions)
Contains at least one named-person usage scenario
